title: Reading Test 4: The Rise of Hybrid Work

passage.label: A
passage.text: Remote work expanded rapidly when many organisations were forced to reduce office attendance. Although some employees have now returned to traditional workplaces, hybrid arrangements remain common in many industries. A hybrid worker may spend part of the week at home and part of the week in an office.

passage.label: B
passage.text: Supporters of hybrid work argue that it offers flexibility. Employees can avoid some commuting, organise focused tasks at home, and attend collaborative meetings in person. Employers may also reduce office costs if fewer desks are needed every day.

passage.label: C
passage.text: However, hybrid work can create communication problems. Informal conversations that happen naturally in an office may be harder to reproduce online. New employees, in particular, may find it more difficult to learn workplace culture if they rarely meet colleagues face to face.

passage.label: D
passage.text: Managers have responded by redesigning meetings and office days. Some teams use shared calendars to identify when people will be present. Others reserve office days for training, planning, and creative tasks that benefit from immediate discussion.

passage.label: E
passage.text: The long-term success of hybrid work depends less on the location of employees than on clear expectations. Organisations need to decide which tasks require physical presence, how performance will be measured, and how workers can remain included even when they are not in the same room.
